title: Cornwall Airport Newquay has begun blending sustainable aviation fuel made from recycled ...
description:
Cornwall Airport Newquay has begun blending sustainable aviation fuel made from recycled restaurant cooking oil into its standard jet fuel supply, part of a growing push across UK regional airports to reduce the aviation sector's carbon footprint without requiring new aircraft technology.
The blended fuel is compatible with existing planes and engines, meaning airlines can adopt it immediately rather than waiting for a fleet-wide transition.
Early figures suggest the switch is cutting lifecycle emissions by hundreds of tonnes.
The approach reflects a broader industry trend toward sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, as one of the few near-term tools available to reduce aviation emissions, an industry notoriously difficult to decarbonize given the energy density required for flight.
Recycled cooking oil is one of the most viable current feedstocks because it repurposes existing waste rather than requiring new agricultural land or resources, though supply remains limited relative to total global jet fuel demand.

text:
India supplied 895 crore litres of ethanol by the end of August under the Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025-26 with grain-based feedstocks accounting for nearly 70 per cent of these cumulative supplies, according to data released by the All India Distillers' Association (AIDA) on Saturday.

According to the data, it is equivalent to around 85 per cent of the 1,048 crore litres contracted for the period.

According to AIDA, grain-based feedstocks contributed 624 crore litres of the total ethanol supplied, while sugar-based feedstocks accounted for 271 crore litres.

Among grain-based sources, maize was the largest contributor with 345 crore litres of ethanol supply. Surplus rice sourced from the Food Corporation of India (FCI) contributed 214 crore litres, while damaged food grains accounted for 64 crore litres.

Within the sugar-based segment, sugarcane juice contributed 149 crore litres by the end of August. B-heavy molasses supplied 107 crore litres and C-heavy molasses contributed 15 crore litres.

AIDA said the figures reflect the increasing diversification of India's ethanol supply ecosystem, reducing dependence on any single feedstock pathway.

Commenting on the data, Bharati Balaji, Deputy Director General, AIDA, said nearly 70 per cent of the 895 crore litres supplied so far has come from grain-based feedstocks, led by maize and surplus FCI rice, while sugar-based sources continue to provide a significant share.

She said the diversity of feedstocks strengthens India's ethanol programme by allowing the industry to utilise multiple domestic agricultural resources.

The association, however, noted that as domestic ethanol production capacity and supplies continue to expand, ensuring adequate and predictable demand avenues will become increasingly important.

According to AIDA, the issue will gain significance as India seeks to move beyond the current ethanol-blending programme and expand ethanol utilisation in flex-fuel vehicles (FFVs), compressed biogas (CBG), sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and other applications.

title: United Airlines CEO pushes for government subsidies for sustainable aviation fuel
description:
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby is pushing the U.S. government to subsidize sustainable aviation fuel the same way it once backed solar and wind power, arguing that early government support builds an industry until it can stand on its own.
"Once you drive down the cost curve, you don't have to have those incentives, but the incentives built the industry and we have to do the same thing for sustainable aviation fuel.
It's the only way it's going to work," he told Colorado Public Radio.
Kirby's pitch also leans on economics beyond climate goals.
Its latest quarterly filing shows the airline holds a 33% ownership stake in the United Airlines Ventures Sustainable Flight Fund, which backs decarbonization technology including sustainable fuel production.

title: Sweden Celebrates SAS at 80 as Scandinavian Airlines Marks 80 Years of Aviation ...
description:
Eight decades of transformation define SAS aviation history Few airlines have experienced such a dramatic transformation as Scandinavian Airlines (SAS).
The 1946 foundation that created a Scandinavian aviation powerhouse The creation of SAS came at a crucial moment in global aviation history.
The achievement strengthened SAS’s reputation as an aviation innovator and placed the Scandinavian carrier at the centre of global aviation development.
SAS and the evolution of global tourism connectivity Over eight decades, SAS has remained closely linked with the development of Scandinavian tourism.
The Nordic region has often been recognised for environmental innovation, and sustainability has become closely linked with Scandinavian aviation identity.
text:
SAS at 80 represents one of aviation’s most remarkable journeys, from pioneering Arctic routes to navigating modern airline challenges. Founded in 1946 through cooperation between Denmark, Norway and Sweden, Scandinavian Airlines became a global aviation innovator by introducing historic polar services and shaping international connectivity. The airline’s eight-decade evolution reflects technological progress, changing passenger expectations and the transformation of the global travel industry. From its first intercontinental operations to today’s sustainability and network strategies, SAS at 80 highlights how a regional carrier built a worldwide reputation while continuing to adapt within an increasingly competitive aviation landscape.

Eight decades of transformation define SAS aviation history

Few airlines have experienced such a dramatic transformation as Scandinavian Airlines (SAS). Celebrating its 80-year milestone, the carrier stands as a symbol of Nordic cooperation, aviation ambition and continuous adaptation. Since its creation in 1946, SAS has moved through several defining eras, including post-war international expansion, pioneering Arctic aviation, the introduction of jet aircraft, digital transformation and the current shift towards more sustainable operations.

The story of SAS at 80 is not only about an airline surviving eight decades of industry change. It is also about how aviation innovation can influence global tourism, business connectivity and passenger mobility. From connecting Scandinavia with North America and Asia to supporting regional economies through international routes, SAS has played an important role in opening Northern Europe to the world.

The airline was created when three Scandinavian aviation companies joined forces: Denmark’s Det Danske Luftfartselskab A/S (DDL), Norway’s Det Norske Luftfartselskap A/S (DNL), and Sweden’s Svensk Intercontinental Lufttrafik AB (SILA). This cooperation created a combined international aviation platform capable of competing in the rapidly developing post-war air travel market.

The formation reflected a wider Scandinavian approach: collaboration could create stronger global influence than separate national efforts. This principle became central to SAS’s identity and helped establish the airline as one of Europe’s most recognised aviation brands.

The 1946 foundation that created a Scandinavian aviation powerhouse

The creation of SAS came at a crucial moment in global aviation history. After the Second World War, international air travel entered a period of rapid expansion as countries rebuilt economies and demand for long-distance journeys increased.

Before SAS existed, Denmark, Norway and Sweden operated separate aviation organisations. However, international routes required greater resources, aircraft capacity and technical expertise. By combining their strengths, the three nations created an airline capable of launching long-range services.

SAS began operations in 1946, with its first intercontinental service connecting Stockholm and New York. This early achievement demonstrated the airline’s ambition to become an international carrier rather than only a regional operator.

The airline quickly focused on improving long-distance travel between Scandinavia and major global markets. During this period, aircraft technology was developing rapidly, and airlines competed to reduce journey times while improving reliability and passenger comfort.

For Scandinavia, international aviation was more than transportation. It represented economic opportunity, allowing businesses, tourists and communities to establish stronger links with North America and other overseas destinations.

SAS becomes the world’s polar aviation pioneer

One of the defining moments in SAS aviation history came in 1954 when the airline achieved a breakthrough that changed commercial aviation forever.

SAS became the first airline to operate a scheduled commercial service using a polar route between Copenhagen and Los Angeles. The route represented a major technological and navigational achievement because flying over Arctic regions required specialised planning, advanced navigation systems and new operational methods.

The historic service demonstrated that polar routes could significantly improve international connectivity by reducing distances between Europe and North America. The achievement strengthened SAS’s reputation as an aviation innovator and placed the Scandinavian carrier at the centre of global aviation development.

The success of the polar route was not simply a publicity achievement. It represented practical progress. Shorter routes meant improved efficiency, reduced flying times and stronger commercial links between continents.

The Arctic environment created unique operational challenges. Aircraft had to operate in remote areas where emergency infrastructure was limited. Navigation, weather forecasting and crew preparation became essential elements of successful polar operations.

By solving these challenges, SAS contributed to aviation knowledge that later influenced long-distance international routes operated by airlines worldwide.

Expanding global connections through pioneering routes

Following the success of its first polar operations, SAS continued developing ambitious international services.

In 1957, the airline introduced another historic achievement by becoming the first carrier to offer a scheduled route around the world over the North Pole, connecting Copenhagen and Tokyo through Anchorage.

This period established SAS as a company willing to explore new possibilities when other airlines were still relying mainly on traditional routes. The airline’s ability to operate in challenging environments helped build a reputation for reliability and technical expertise.

The expansion also supported tourism growth. Faster connections between Scandinavia, North America and Asia created new opportunities for leisure travellers, business visitors and cultural exchange.

During the 1950s, international tourism was beginning to expand beyond wealthy travellers and diplomats. Airlines like SAS helped make long-distance travel increasingly accessible by improving route networks and operational efficiency.

The airline’s Scandinavian identity also became an important part of its global appeal. The carrier promoted Nordic design, hospitality and service principles, creating a distinctive passenger experience.

Entering the jet age and modernising aviation operations

The late 1950s marked another major transformation for SAS as the airline entered the jet era.

In 1959, SAS introduced its first jet aircraft, the Caravelle, marking a new phase in speed, efficiency and passenger comfort.

Jet technology changed commercial aviation by dramatically reducing travel times and allowing airlines to expand international networks. For SAS, adopting new aircraft reflected its long-standing focus on innovation.

The transition from propeller aircraft to jets allowed the airline to strengthen its position in international aviation. Passengers could travel faster between continents, while airlines could operate more efficient schedules.

The introduction of new aircraft also changed airport infrastructure, maintenance requirements and crew training. SAS invested in these areas to support its expanding operations.

This period reinforced a pattern that would continue throughout the airline’s history: adapting early to technological change.

Building a Scandinavian service identity

Beyond aircraft and routes, SAS developed a reputation around passenger experience.

The airline became associated with Scandinavian design, efficiency and attention to customer service. These values helped differentiate SAS in a competitive aviation market where airlines increasingly focused on creating unique identities.

The concept of combining functional design with passenger comfort became part of the wider Scandinavian approach to travel. Cabin environments, airport services and operational standards reflected Nordic principles of simplicity and practicality.

SAS also expanded beyond aviation through related hospitality initiatives. The opening of SAS Royal Hotel Copenhagen in 1960 became another example of the company’s broader approach to travel experiences.

The hotel connected aviation, accommodation and design, creating an integrated travel concept during a period when tourism industries were becoming increasingly interconnected.

SAS and the evolution of global tourism connectivity

Over eight decades, SAS has remained closely linked with the development of Scandinavian tourism.

The airline’s international network helped bring visitors to Denmark, Norway and Sweden while also enabling Nordic residents to explore global destinations.

Air connectivity plays a vital role in tourism growth. Direct routes reduce travel barriers, encourage international visitor flows and strengthen economic relationships between destinations.

For Scandinavian economies, aviation connectivity has supported industries including hospitality, conferences, trade and cultural tourism.

The role of SAS extends beyond transporting passengers. Like many national and regional carriers, the airline has contributed to destination visibility by maintaining international links and promoting Scandinavia as a connected travel region.

The Jan Carlzon era reshaped SAS into a customer-focused airline

One of the most influential periods in SAS aviation history came during the 1980s under the leadership of Jan Carlzon, who became president and CEO of SAS in 1981.

At a time when airlines worldwide were facing increasing competition, economic uncertainty and changing passenger expectations, SAS introduced a new approach focused on customer experience and operational efficiency.

Carlzon’s leadership philosophy placed passengers at the centre of airline operations. The strategy became widely recognised through the concept of the “Moments of Truth”, which highlighted every interaction between customers and the company as an opportunity to create value.

The approach transformed how SAS viewed service delivery. Instead of focusing only on aircraft operations, the airline concentrated on improving the entire passenger journey, from booking and airport services to onboard experiences.

This customer-focused strategy helped SAS strengthen its reputation as an innovative European carrier and influenced wider airline management practices.

The period demonstrated that aviation success depended not only on technology and networks but also on understanding traveller expectations.

For the tourism industry, these changes reflected a broader shift. Travellers were becoming more experienced and demanding, expecting reliability, comfort and personalised service alongside competitive prices.

SAS responded by positioning itself as a premium airline with strong Scandinavian values.

SAS joins global aviation cooperation through Star Alliance

The next major milestone in the airline’s international development came in 1997 when SAS became one of the founding members of Star Alliance, the world’s first global airline alliance.

The creation of Star Alliance represented a major change in the aviation industry. Airlines increasingly recognised that cooperation could improve global connectivity without requiring complete mergers or ownership integration.

Through alliance partnerships, SAS passengers gained access to a wider international network, while partner airlines strengthened their presence in Scandinavian markets.

For travellers, airline alliances created smoother connections, coordinated schedules and improved loyalty benefits.

The development was particularly important for business travel and long-distance tourism, where passengers often required multiple airline connections to reach destinations worldwide.

SAS’s participation reflected its long-standing international ambition. The airline that had once pioneered polar routes was now becoming part of a global aviation ecosystem.

The alliance model also supported tourism growth by making destinations more accessible. Visitors could travel more efficiently between continents, supporting international visitor flows and economic exchange.

Digital transformation changes the passenger experience

As aviation entered the digital era, SAS continued adapting its operations to new technologies.

The airline invested in online services, mobile solutions and digital customer platforms designed to make travel more convenient.

Modern travellers increasingly expect digital access throughout their journey, including online booking, mobile check-in, travel updates and self-service airport processes.

text:
Two clocks are running at Bayer, and they tick at wildly different speeds. One is measured in days: on Monday, Judge Timothy Boyer in St. Louis will decide whether to grant final approval to the EUR 7.25 billion settlement Bayer struck in February to resolve the bulk of its Roundup litigation. The other runs in years — the slow, deliberate build-out of an agricultural franchise that management hopes will eventually stand on its own, free of the toxicology debates that have shadowed the company for the better part of a decade.

The courtroom drama is the nearer-term catalyst, but the details that have surfaced in recent days matter more than the hearing itself. A preliminary court session roughly two weeks ago knocked 1.7 percent off the share price, yet the real news lies in how the payout structure is staggered — and what that staggering reveals about the true financial exposure.

Who gets what, and why it matters

The agreement covers some 65,000 US claims tied to non-Hodgkin lymphoma and alleged exposure to the herbicide before February 17, 2026 — regardless of whether a diagnosis has already been made. Payouts are tiered by age, occupational exposure, and how aggressive the disease is. Average awards range from about USD 10,000 at the low end to USD 165,000 at the top. In the highest bracket — plaintiffs under 60 with occupational exposure and an aggressive disease course — a points-based system can push individual payments as high as USD 198,000.

At the other extreme sit so-called quick-pay tiers with fixed sums of between USD 6,000 and USD 14,500, plus a limited-evidence category that pays just USD 150. Claimants who already have a diagnosis will have 180 days from final approval to register.

That laddering is precisely why the headline figure of USD 7.25 billion shouldn't be read as an even split across all claimants. A large share of cases is likely to land in the lower and middle tiers, which makes the ultimate burden more predictable than a flat per-plaintiff settlement would suggest. The opt-out window for claimants who wanted to reject the deal and litigate individually closed on June 4 — a signal that participation levels were largely locked in well before Boyer rules.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Bayer?

A market that has already made up its mind

Equity investors, for their part, appear to have priced in approval. Bayer closed Friday at EUR 48.19, down 0.6 percent on the day and about 1.3 percent over the week. That leaves the stock roughly 11 percent below its 52-week high of EUR 53.86, set in July, but still far above the EUR 25.78 trough from last November. Over the past twelve months, the shares have climbed 67 percent — a run that suggests much of the legal risk is already baked in. The muted reaction to earlier procedural steps reinforces the view that most traders expect Boyer to sign off.

Should approval come through as planned, one of the longest-running overhangs on the stock would finally be retired. A rejection or a delay, on the other hand, would raise fresh questions about how Bayer has calculated its provisions — particularly for the thousands of claims that have yet to be diagnosed but fall within the settlement's scope. An RSI reading of 47.4 points to neutral sentiment; the market is waiting for a firmer signal.

The quieter story: rapeseed, biofuels, and a Finnish partner

While the courtroom commands attention, a second narrative has been taking shape on the agricultural side. Bayer and Neste — the Finnish group that bills itself as the world's leading producer of biodiesel and sustainable aviation fuel — plan to scale Bayer's newgold® winter rapeseed as a feedstock for biofuels. The initial focus is the Southern Great Plains of the United States, with commercial launch of the TruFlex winter rapeseed hybrids slated for autumn 2027.

The timing is deliberate. Bayer is trying to reposition its crop business as a dependable growth driver, and the Neste tie-up lands alongside the legal relief from the Supreme Court's June 25 ruling in the Durnell case, which established that federal law preempts state-level failure-to-warn claims.

Whether the partnership becomes a genuine earnings pillar comes down to a single metric: the margin Crop Science can extract from specialty seeds like newgold®. In the second quarter of 2026, the division delivered the group's strongest growth impulse with a 30.2 percent jump in adjusted earnings, while the pharmaceutical unit slipped 3.6 percent. If that trajectory holds and newgold® opens an additional sales channel into the biofuel market, Crop Science could become a structural counterweight to the thinner-margin pharma business.

Two paths, one stock

The bull case writes itself: a structurally expanding market for sustainable fuels, a portfolio that doesn't lean on toxicologically contested active ingredients, a net financial debt forecast already trimmed for 2026 to between EUR 29 billion and EUR 30 billion on the back of the capital injection from the Apollo partnership, and a confirmed full-year outlook of EUR 9.6 billion to EUR 10.1 billion in adjusted EBITDA. Add further revenue contributions from the oncology pipeline — including sevabertinib — and the stock could be nudged back toward its annual high.

Bayer at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.

The bear case is just as coherent. The Neste arrangement could remain a letter of intent for years before any revenue materializes in 2027. Core EPS already fell 16.7 percent year-on-year in the second quarter, weighed down by higher marketing spend in pharma. If that pressure persists, a multi-year agricultural project offers little near-term relief. And the glyphosate question isn't fully settled even with the Supreme Court ruling: the fairness hearing on the USD 7.25 billion settlement was pushed to September 14 after the court needed time to process revocation requests tied to the opt-out deadline.

What to watch

As long as Crop Science sustains its second-quarter momentum and the Neste partnership advances toward its 2027 launch without delays, the market is likely to treat the agricultural segment as an increasingly stabilizing force. Should that momentum falter — through another disappointing pharma quarter or fresh holdups in Missouri — the shares could stay range-bound between the 50-day moving average of EUR 48.57 and the 52-week high.

The September 14 fairness hearing is the next concrete date on which this question will sharpen. Its outcome will help determine how much attention the market is willing to spare for the longer-term agricultural story — and whether Bayer's two clocks finally start running in the same direction.

Haffner Energy is well known for designing and supplying innovative solutions for the production of competitive renewable fuels for biomass. With over 33 years experience, using different types of biomass, the company has developed proprietary thermolysis and gasification technologies permitting the production of renewable gas, hydrogen, renewable methanol, power, and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

When energy companies decide to collaborate, it is highly important that they complement each other effectively to ensure they meet their overall targets. OroCarbo is mainly involved in research and development of technologies and business ventures that are connected to biofuels, biochar, graphite, and graphene, including its biomass raw materials, processing equipment, technology, and more.

OroCarbo reserves 12 Haffner systems for a string of renewable hydrogen hubs

CORE100 is Haffner Energy’s industrial program for the deployment of the first 100 standardized C-iC units. The program is designed to quicken commercial deployment through standardization and series production. It allows customers to reserve production slots for modular units that can be deployed individually or combined to serve larger projects.

A recent press release from Haffner Energy unveiled that the company seeks to deploy the units as part of its development of local renewable energy hubs in California, Oregon, and Washington State. The products are expected to convert locally available residual biomass into renewable syngas, mainly for renewable hydrogen for mobility and local power generation in areas where grid capacity and reliability may be restricted.

The Haffner Energy officials believe that the reservation for 12 CiC units represents a new step in its partnership with OroCarbo which is the roll out of the company’s CORE100 across the Western United States. This relationship is one that may bring many captivating projects to the industry.

Both companies are pleased following the announcement of their most recent collaboration. Brian Wong, Founder and Managing Member of OroCarbo, stated:

“Our ambition is to develop local renewable energy hubs that turn abundant residual biomass into clean energy where it is needed. We see significant opportunities both for renewable hydrogen in mobility and for local power generation in areas where grid capacity or reliability is a constraint. Reserving 12 SYNOCA® C-iC units is an important step towards building that network with Haffner Energy.”

text:
This is a reduced version of The Business Times’ ESG Insights newsletter. Sign up here to get the complete version in your inbox every week.

💡This week: Singapore’s decision to delay a green jet fuel levy for air cargo is the latest challenge confronting efforts to decarbonise the aviation sector.

The sector is veering further in the wrong direction with regards to sustainable aviation fuel, and it seems increasingly likely that the industry will have to adopt more realistic targets or accept widespread non-compliance. If that happens, investors in the sector may face higher-for-longer emissions in their portfolios as well as greater uncertainty about climate transition risks.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) has announced that a planned sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) levy for air cargo will be deferred for one year, such that it will now apply to services sold from Oct 1, 2027 for flights that depart Singapore from Jan 1, 2028. The exact levy amounts are based on the prevailing price premiums of SAF over fossil-based jet fuel and route distances.

This is the second levy deferment for air cargo, after the aviation regulator’s March 2026 announcement of a six-month delay on the original plan to impose the levy for all passenger and cargo flights sold from April 2026 for flights departing Singapore starting Oct 1, 2026. There is no second deferment for passenger flights, which will begin to include the levy starting Oct 1 for flights departing Jan 1, 2027 onwards.

CAAS says that, compared to passenger operations, air cargo operations are more diverse and involve a wider spectrum of stakeholders. The delay takes into account industry feedback that it needs more time to work with CAAS to develop and implement a robust SAF levy collecting mechanism for cargo flights. Singapore has estimated that cargo SAF levies could be around S$0.01 to S$0.15 per kilogramme of cargo, depending on the length of the route.

CAAS granted the original March deferment as a response to disruptions arising from the Iran war.

The SAF levy is a critical piece in Singapore’s strategy for greening its aviation sector, with a goal of achieving a one per cent SAF uplift in 2026 en route to a 3-to-5 per cent uplift by 2030, subject to global developments and SAF availability. The levy collections will be channelled to a statutory SAF fund that will act as a central buyer of SAF for flights departing from Singapore. The policy thesis is that a consolidated central buyer can obtain better prices for plane operators, as well as provide a clearer demand signal for SAF producers.

It is clear that the 2026 uplift target will not be achieved. The 2030 goal could still be in play, but the delays mean that Singapore will have to raise the pace of uplift more rapidly than initially hoped, which might face resistance from plane operators going through the country.

All this attention to SAF has its roots in global efforts to decarbonise aviation, which contributes about 2 to 3 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. SAF is a key pillar in the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) target of net zero greenhouse emissions for international aviation – which contributes about 1.5 per cent of global emissions – by 2050.

In support of that goal, the industry’s International Air Transport Association (Iata) has set a target of raising SAF to 65 per cent of the fuel mix by 2050. However, Iata’s latest estimate is that global SAF production will represent only about 0.8 per cent – or 2.4 million tonnes – of total fuel use in 2026 despite having five years to try to raise the percentage since the targets were adopted. Furthermore, SAF is still about two to five times as expensive as fossil jet fuel.

Iata director general William Walsh says: “The path to meeting 65 per cent of our needs in 2050 is growing more difficult with each year of ineffectively sequenced government policies and oil companies’ manifest lack of interest. The current energy shock should add even more urgency to the development of renewables, including SAF. But we have yet to see either the energy shock, the need to develop energy independence and jobs, or the urgency to mitigate climate change materialise in the incentives needed to create a viable SAF market.”

Iata also takes issue with attempts in Europe to mandate production of electro-SAF (e-SAF), which refers to SAF produced using renewable electricity, water and captured carbon dioxide instead of biomass. Production mandates in the European Union and United Kingdom are “utterly detached from reality” because they require supply to balloon without supporting that level of growth, says Marie Owens Thomsen, Iata’s chief economist and senior vice-president of sustainability.

But even if policymakers pull the right levers – and even if Singapore’s levy-and-centralised procurement strategy proves effective in helping to propel production while keeping SAF prices viable – there remains a question of whether it makes sense to bank so much of aviation’s decarbonisation on SAF.

A 2025 academic paper by French researchers Paul Bardon and Olivier Massol argues that aviation decarbonisation cannot rely on SAF at scale. The researchers observe that the aviation industry has never been able to meet its SAF goals. A 2008 target for 10 per cent SAF incorporation by 2017 was reduced in 2019 to 2 per cent by 2025, and progress towards the current goal remains elusive.

While Bardon and Massol acknowledge that better policies can help to drive more investments into SAF, they note limitations in the availability of biofeedstock. Allocating resources towards SAF production at the scale required to achieve net zero by 2050 will probably slow the decarbonisation of other sectors.

For example, using renewable energy to replace coal power, for electric vehicles or for heat pumps would be a more efficient way to decarbonise than producing e-SAF, the authors say, citing the British Climate Change Committee.

“In light of the unfairness and inefficiency of such a policy, this study argues that granting aviation priority over the industry-forecasted amounts of critical resources in 2050 is neither sensible nor fundamentally feasible,” the paper states.

The reality is that the aviation sector’s current decarbonisation goals do not appear to be realistic. To keep the goals credible, the industry will probably have to recalibrate. However, doing so will take the sector out of alignment with pathways for net zero by 2050.

This could create challenges for investors – especially institutional players – that have their own decarbonisation goals for their portfolios. For instance, Singapore’s Temasek has cited its stake in Singapore Airlines as a reason why it is likely to miss its 2030 target for portfolio emissions.

Being behind the decarbonisation curve also raises the risk of aviation players being on the wrong side of future climate-related policies. For example, an airline could face lower margins or lower ticket sales if policymakers tax their emissions more aggressively.

In fact, Bardon and Massol argue that policies “constraining the sector’s growth” are necessary to achieve net zero.

“Aviation can achieve decarbonisation only through a more sustainable air traffic growth associated with reasonable resource utilisation,” the authors write.

Egypt’s Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources (MoPMR) discussed cooperation with Kenya to exchange expertise in green manufacturing, biofuels, energy efficiency and emissions reduction, as both sides seek closer coordination on energy and climate projects.

The talks took place during a visit by Ali Mohamed, Special Envoy of the President of Kenya for Climate Change, who met Mahmoud Nagy, Undersecretary at the Ministry overseeing environment, safety, energy efficiency and climate affairs and the ministry’s spokesperson.

Officials from the Egyptian Petrochemicals Holding Company (ECHEM) and members of the ministry’s energy efficiency and climate team also attended.

The discussions covered carbon emissions reduction, energy efficiency, circular economy practices and ways to share technical experience between Egypt and Kenya.

The ministry presented Egypt’s work on improving operational efficiency, cutting emissions and expanding green manufacturing practices across the petroleum and petrochemical sectors.

ECHEM officials also reviewed projects under development, including sustainable aviation fuel from used cooking oil, bioethanol production, green ammonia and low-carbon urea fertilizers.

The Kenyan side presented its experience in geothermal power generation, with both parties discussing possible technical cooperation and knowledge exchange in the sector.

Both sides agreed to continue coordination through Egypt’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs to advance the areas discussed.

The talks build on Egypt’s expanding biofuel projects. In October 2025, ECHEM secured $135 million in long-term financing for the Egyptian Bioethanol Company’s Damietta project, which targets annual production of 100,000 tons of low-emission biofuel using sugar beet molasses as feedstock.

The project is expected to support domestic biofuel production and reduce emissions while supplying fuel and industrial applications.

title: Port of Açu Sustainable Fuels Terminal Planned by 2030 - Bioenergy Business
description:
According to Port of Açu CEO Eugênio Figueiredo, the strategy is to combine fuel production and cargo handling at the port.
Port expands focus beyond sustainable fuels Açu’s energy transition programme also includes changes to how the port itself consumes energy and operates its marine assets.
Bioenergy Business Analysis The Port of Açu’s planned sustainable fuels terminal reflects an infrastructure-led approach to the energy transition.
Açu’s plans extend beyond the proposed sustainable fuels terminal.
For now, the sustainable fuels terminal remains a development-stage project.
text:
Brazil’s Port of Açu is planning a dedicated sustainable fuels terminal as it seeks to expand its role in the country’s energy transition, with green methanol, green ammonia, sustainable aviation fuel and biomethane among the fuels targeted by the development.

The project is part of the Port of Açu’s priority investment portfolio through 2030, although the planned infrastructure remains subject to environmental licensing and does not yet have a defined completion date.

Port aims to integrate fuel production and handling

Located in northern Rio de Janeiro state, the Port of Açu intends to bring multiple stages of the sustainable fuels value chain within its existing industrial complex.

According to Port of Açu CEO Eugênio Figueiredo, the strategy is to combine fuel production and cargo handling at the port. The planned terminal would support the production of green methanol, green ammonia and SAF using green hydrogen, alongside biomethane.

Açu’s existing liquids terminal is expected to play a role in the development by providing storage for the resulting fuels. The area will also be expanded to accommodate green fuel production.

The approach would give the port a role extending beyond conventional cargo handling, positioning it as an integrated location for the production, storage and movement of lower-carbon fuels.

Environmental licensing remains a key milestone

The sustainable fuels terminal is still undergoing environmental licensing, meaning the project has not yet reached a stage where a firm construction or completion schedule can be established.

Nevertheless, the development remains part of Açu’s priority investment plans through 2030. The absence of a defined completion deadline means the timing of individual structures will depend on the licensing and development process.

The planned fuel mix reflects several emerging areas of demand across the energy and transport sectors. Green ammonia and green methanol can serve as alternative fuels for maritime and industrial applications, while SAF is being developed as a lower-carbon aviation fuel.

In Brazil, the Port of Açu expects SAF demand to gain momentum from 2027, when national aviation emissions-reduction targets are scheduled to begin taking effect.

Port expands focus beyond sustainable fuels

Açu’s energy transition programme also includes changes to how the port itself consumes energy and operates its marine assets.

The complex has started testing ethanol as a lower-emission fuel alternative for smaller vessels. The initiative forms part of a broader effort to reduce emissions from port operations while evaluating technologies and fuels that could potentially be deployed more widely.

Berth electrification is another project under development. The objective is to allow ships to use electricity while docked during loading and unloading rather than keeping their engines running throughout their stay at the quay.

The port plans to initially focus on smaller vessels and equipment before potentially extending electrification to larger ships as the necessary technology and infrastructure develop.

Testing has already taken place at the terminal’s offshore berth, including trials involving tugboats, according to Figueiredo. At the port’s main berth, electrification remains under study.

The expansion into sustainable fuels is taking place alongside Açu’s established role in Brazil’s oil sector. The port currently handles about 40% of the country’s oil exports. Figueiredo also expects oil exports through the complex to increase significantly in the coming years.

A new liquids terminal is currently under construction, with completion expected in approximately 45 days. The facility will include storage areas for lubricants and marine fuels.

Vibra Energia is expected to be the first company to operate at the new terminal, according to Figueiredo.

This means Açu’s energy strategy is developing across both conventional and emerging fuels rather than replacing its existing oil-related activities with sustainable fuels in the near term.

Bioenergy Business Analysis

The Port of Açu’s planned sustainable fuels terminal reflects an infrastructure-led approach to the energy transition. Rather than focusing on a single fuel, the port is considering a portfolio spanning green hydrogen derivatives, SAF and biomethane while also examining electrification and lower-emission fuels for its own operations.

The combination of sustainable fuel production and port infrastructure could nevertheless be commercially relevant because it connects fuel manufacturing with an established logistics and cargo-handling environment. For fuel developers, the development highlights the importance of locations that can accommodate both production and downstream movement of emerging low-carbon fuels.

Açu’s plans extend beyond the proposed sustainable fuels terminal. Ethanol trials, berth electrification and continued investment in liquids infrastructure indicate that the port is pursuing several routes to reduce or manage emissions while maintaining its existing energy-sector business.

For now, the sustainable fuels terminal remains a development-stage project. Environmental licensing and subsequent investment decisions will determine how the proposed green methanol, green ammonia, SAF and biomethane activities progress towards implementation.

text:
India supplied 895 crore litres of ethanol by the end of August 2026, against a contracted quantity of 1,048 crore litres for Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025-26, according to data compiled by the All India Distillers’ Association (AIDA). This represents around 85% of the contracted volume.

Grain-based feedstocks accounted for 624 crore litres, or nearly 70% of cumulative supplies, while sugar-based feedstocks contributed 271 crore litres. The data indicates a larger contribution from grain-based production pathways within the overall ethanol supply mix.

Within the grain-based segment, maize was the largest individual feedstock, contributing 345 crore litres. Surplus Food Corporation of India (FCI) rice accounted for 214 crore litres, while damaged food grains contributed 64 crore litres.

Grain-Based Ethanol Accounts For Nearly 70% Of Supplies

Of the 895 crore litres supplied by August-end, 624 crore litres came from grain-based feedstocks, compared with 271 crore litres from sugar-based sources. The grain-based allocation for the year stood at 760 crore litres, according to the AIDA data table, against 624 crore litres supplied by August-end.

Maize's 345 crore litre contribution made it the largest contributor among all individual feedstocks. Surplus FCI rice followed with 214 crore litres, while damaged food grains accounted for 64 crore litres.

The data also points to the use of multiple agricultural resources in ethanol production. AIDA said the wider feedstock base allows production to draw on different agricultural sources depending on availability, providing greater flexibility to the supply chain.

Sugar-Based Ethanol Supplies Reach 271 Crore Litres

Sugar-based feedstocks contributed 271 crore litres by August-end. Sugarcane juice accounted for 149 crore litres, followed by B Heavy Molasses at 107 crore litres and C Heavy Molasses at 15 crore litres.

AIDA said the continued contribution from both grain- and sugar-based pathways supports a multi-feedstock approach as the ethanol programme moves into its next phase.

Ethanol Supplies Reach 85% Of Contracted Volume

The industry supplied 895 crore litres against 1,048 crore litres contracted for ESY 2025-26 by August-end, leaving 153 crore litres of the contracted quantity yet to be supplied.

AIDA said the next issue for the sector will increasingly be matching growth in ethanol production with sufficient and predictable avenues for utilisation. It identified Flex-Fuel Vehicles (FFVs), compressed biogas (CBG), sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and other applications as potential demand avenues as India looks beyond the current blending framework.

AIDA Deputy Director General Bharati Balaji said the August-end figures show that grain-based feedstocks have become a significant part of the supply mix, while sugar-based sources continue to provide a substantial volume. She said the diversification reduces reliance on a single feedstock pathway.

Balaji also said the sector's focus would need to increasingly shift towards utilisation of the production and supply capacity already established. According to her, additional demand from FFVs, CBG, SAF and other ethanol applications, alongside a predictable policy framework, would be important for supporting continued investment and the wider use of the available capacity.

Key Ethanol Supply Numbers For August 2026

AIDA's August-end data shows that grain-based and sugar-based feedstocks are both contributing to India's domestic ethanol supply, with grain-based sources accounting for the larger share so far in ESY 2025-26. The association said the next phase will require alignment between feedstock availability, production capacity and end-use demand.

title: Kemnaker Ajak Generasi Muda Jambi Manfaatkan AI untuk Tingkatkan Produktivitas
description:
Menurut Afriansyah, perkembangan AI, otomatisasi, dan teknologi digital telah mengubah cara kerja di berbagai sektor.
Untuk membantu generasi muda mempersiapkan kompetensi yang sesuai dengan perkembangan dunia kerja, Kemnaker terus menjalankan berbagai program peningkatan kompetensi.
Menurut Afriansyah, kesiapan generasi muda juga perlu didukung keterhubungan antara pembelajaran di perguruan tinggi dan kebutuhan dunia industri.
Keterhubungan tersebut membutuhkan dukungan berbagai pihak, mulai dari pemerintah, perguruan tinggi, industri, komunitas, hingga media, untuk membangun ekosistem ketenagakerjaan yang mendukung kesiapan generasi muda.
Generasi muda diharapkan mampu memanfaatkan perkembangan teknologi, termasuk AI, untuk meningkatkan produktivitas dan mengambil peran dalam perubahan dunia kerja serta pembangunan Indonesia.
text:
JAMBI — Wakil Menteri Ketenagakerjaan (Wamenaker) Afriansyah Noor mengajak generasi muda memanfaatkan kecerdasan buatan atau artificial intelligence (AI) untuk meningkatkan produktivitas sekaligus mempersiapkan kompetensi menghadapi perubahan dunia kerja yang berlangsung cepat.

Menurut Afriansyah, perkembangan AI, otomatisasi, dan teknologi digital telah mengubah cara kerja di berbagai sektor. Perubahan tersebut perlu direspons generasi muda dengan terus mengembangkan kompetensi dan kemampuan beradaptasi agar teknologi dapat dimanfaatkan sebagai peluang dalam dunia kerja.

“Jangan takut pada AI, tapi jangan sampai tertinggal oleh AI. Jadikan teknologi sebagai alat pengganda produktivitas kalian,” kata Afriansyah saat memberikan kuliah umum di Universitas Batanghari, Jambi, Sabtu (12/9/2026).

Ia mengatakan, kemampuan yang dibutuhkan di dunia kerja tidak hanya ditentukan oleh ijazah, tetapi juga kompetensi, karakter, dan kemauan untuk terus belajar. Karena itu, kesiapan menghadapi perubahan dunia kerja perlu dibangun sejak masih menempuh pendidikan.

Tantangan tersebut menjadi semakin penting di tengah besarnya jumlah angkatan kerja nasional. Berdasarkan data BPS Februari 2026, jumlah angkatan kerja Indonesia mencapai 154,91 juta orang dengan tingkat pengangguran sebesar 4,68 persen. Sementara itu, 19,44 persen pemuda usia 15–24 tahun berada dalam kondisi NEET, yaitu tidak bekerja, tidak sedang menempuh pendidikan, maupun mengikuti pelatihan.

Afriansyah juga mengajak generasi muda mengembangkan pola pikir dari sekadar pencari kerja menjadi pencipta kerja. Penguasaan kompetensi dan pemanfaatan teknologi dapat menjadi modal untuk menyelesaikan berbagai persoalan sekaligus membuka peluang baru.

Untuk membantu generasi muda mempersiapkan kompetensi yang sesuai dengan perkembangan dunia kerja, Kemnaker terus menjalankan berbagai program peningkatan kompetensi. Program tersebut antara lain Pelatihan Vokasi Nasional (PVN), Program Magang Nasional (MagangHub), Talent and Innovation Hub (TIH) Pembinaan Talenta Vokasi Indonesia, serta pelatihan melalui Balai Pelatihan Vokasi dan Produktivitas (BPVP).

Menurut Afriansyah, kesiapan generasi muda juga perlu didukung keterhubungan antara pembelajaran di perguruan tinggi dan kebutuhan dunia industri. Kampus tidak hanya berperan dalam pengembangan ilmu, tetapi juga perlu membekali mahasiswa dengan karakter, kompetensi, kemampuan beradaptasi, dan kewirausahaan.

Keterhubungan tersebut membutuhkan dukungan berbagai pihak, mulai dari pemerintah, perguruan tinggi, industri, komunitas, hingga media, untuk membangun ekosistem ketenagakerjaan yang mendukung kesiapan generasi muda.

Upaya meningkatkan kualitas sumber daya manusia tersebut sejalan dengan RPJMN 2025–2029 dalam membangun sumber daya manusia yang adaptif dan berdaya saing global. Generasi muda diharapkan mampu memanfaatkan perkembangan teknologi, termasuk AI, untuk meningkatkan produktivitas dan mengambil peran dalam perubahan dunia kerja serta pembangunan Indonesia.*

text:
TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Director of Insight at the Kadin Indonesia Institute, Fakhrul Fulvian, stated that global oil prices approaching US$100 per barrel make the B50 biofuel agenda increasingly strategic.

The Kadin Indonesia Institute views B50 not merely as an energy policy and import substitution measure, but as a catalyst for transforming domestic industry and strengthening Indonesia's balance of payments.

According to Fakhrul, government estimates indicate that implementing B50 could displace roughly 18 million kiloliters of imported diesel and yield foreign exchange savings of approximately Rp170 trillion. Consequently, Fakhrul noted that these savings would lessen Indonesia's vulnerability to oil price volatility and reduce dependence on external financing.

“So far, when the balance of payments comes under pressure, discussions heavily center on how to draw dollars into Indonesia. B50 operates in the opposite direction, curbing dollar outflows while converting domestic resources into national energy capacity,” he said in a written statement released on Friday, September 11, 2026.

He emphasized that the next challenge is ensuring that the domestic demand generated by B50 fosters a new industrial ecosystem, ranging from refining, storage, terminals, blending, logistics, engineering, testing, to domestic equipment manufacturing.

“We must not only replace imported diesel with domestic feedstock. The benchmark of industrial transformation lies in how much new engineering, technology, logistics, and industrial capabilities are ultimately built within Indonesia,” he added.

Therefore, Fakhrul stated that the Kadin Indonesia Institute is advocating for the formulation of a B50 Industrial Transformation Roadmap. The framework would not only establish blending targets, but also map out the development of feedstock, refining capacity, distribution infrastructure, machinery readiness, domestic equipment, and advanced biofuels such as sustainable aviation fuel.

Fakhrul stressed that B50 implementation must account for end-user sectors, including mining, plantations, trucking, shipping, and heavy-equipment industries. He urged the government to monitor fuel efficiency, maintenance expenses, operational downtime, and equipment reliability following the rollout.

“The foreign exchange savings are substantial, but we must ensure there are no hidden costs in the form of elevated maintenance, downtime, or reduced productivity. B50 must be evaluated based on its net economic benefit for Indonesia,” he said.

State Budget Pressures and Subsidized Fuel

Separately, Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Bahlil Lahadalia responded to global oil prices exceeding US$108.68 per barrel. Bahlil acknowledged that the uptick in crude prices continues to strain state finances.

“This is certainly not a light matter. It is heavy, as subsidy expenditures will undoubtedly rise,” Bahlil told reporters at his office in Jakarta on Friday, September 11, 2026.

He noted that with global oil prices surpassing US$100 per barrel, the average Indonesian Crude Price (ICP) pegged in the 2026 State Budget from January to September sits between US$80 and US$90 per barrel. The benchmark ICP set in the 2026 State Budget is US$70 per barrel.

Calculations by the Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs indicate that every one-dollar increase in the ICP adds Rp10.3 trillion in oil spending.

Conversely, a US$1 per barrel increase boosts state revenues by approximately Rp3.6 trillion, derived from non-tax state revenues (PNBP) in the oil and gas sector.

Nevertheless, Bahlil reaffirmed that the government will not raise subsidized fuel prices. He explained that under President Prabowo Subianto's direction, keeping subsidized fuel prices stable aims to protect public purchasing power.

“President Prabowo believes that safeguarding the purchasing power of lower- and middle-income groups is far more important, even amid the measures we must undertake. Expanding the subsidy budget, I think, is part of the steps we take,” Bahlil said.

Nandito Putra contributed to this article

title: India's ethanol supply hits 895 crore litres in August; grains contribute nearly 70 pc: Report
description:
"India’s ethanol supply ecosystem is becoming increasingly diversified, with grain-based feedstocks contributing 624 crore litres of ethanol by the end of August 2026, accounting for nearly 70% of cumulative supplies under Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025-26," the release said adding, “Of the 895 crore litres supplied cumulatively by August-end, 624 crore litres came from grain-based feedstocks, while sugar-based feedstocks contributed 271 crore litres."
Among grain-based feedstocks, maize was the largest contributor, supplying 345 crore litres of ethanol, followed by surplus Food Corporation of India (FCI) rice at 214 crore litres and damaged food grains at 64 crore litres.
At the same time, sugar-based feedstocks contributed 271 crore litres by August-end.
“Within this, Sugarcane Juice contributed 149 crore litres, followed by B Heavy Molasses at 107 crore litres and C Heavy Molasses at 15 crore litres,” it noted.
Nearly 70% of the 895 crore litres supplied so far has come from grain-based feedstocks, with maize contributing 345 crore litres and surplus FCI rice contributing another 214 crore litres.
text:
New Delhi [India], September 12 (ANI): Grain-based feedstocks have emerged as the dominant source of India’s ethanol supply, contributing nearly 70 per cent of cumulative supplies, under the Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025-26 as of August 2026, according to data compiled by the All India Distillers’ Association (AIDA).As per the data shared by AIDA, India’s overall ethanol supplies reached 895 crore litres by the end of August, representing around 85 per cent of the 1,048 crore litres contracted. "India’s ethanol supply ecosystem is becoming increasingly diversified, with grain-based feedstocks contributing 624 crore litres of ethanol by the end of August 2026, accounting for nearly 70% of cumulative supplies under Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025-26," the release said adding, “Of the 895 crore litres supplied cumulatively by August-end, 624 crore litres came from grain-based feedstocks, while sugar-based feedstocks contributed 271 crore litres."

Among grain-based feedstocks, maize was the largest contributor, supplying 345 crore litres of ethanol, followed by surplus Food Corporation of India (FCI) rice at 214 crore litres and damaged food grains at 64 crore litres. At the same time, sugar-based feedstocks contributed 271 crore litres by August-end. “Within this, Sugarcane Juice contributed 149 crore litres, followed by B Heavy Molasses at 107 crore litres and C Heavy Molasses at 15 crore litres,” it noted. However, the release noted, “as domestic ethanol capacity and supply continue to expand, the next challenge will increasingly be to ensure that production growth is matched by adequate and predictable avenues for utilisation.” According to the release, this will become increasingly important as India moves beyond the existing ethanol-blending framework towards wider use in Flex-Fuel Vehicles (FFVs), Compressed Biogas (CBG), Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and other applications.Bharati Balaji, Deputy Director General, All India Distillers’ Association (AIDA), said, “The August-end numbers demonstrate how significantly India’s ethanol supply ecosystem has evolved. Nearly 70% of the 895 crore litres supplied so far has come from grain-based feedstocks, with maize contributing 345 crore litres and surplus FCI rice contributing another 214 crore litres. At the same time, sugar-based feedstocks continue to provide a substantial share of supplies. This diversity is an important strength of India’s ethanol programme, as it enables the industry to draw upon multiple domestic agricultural resources and reduces dependence on any single feedstock pathway.” (ANI)

text:
OMV Petrom invested approximately EUR 115 million to modernize the electrical infrastructure of the Petrobrazi refinery. The investment is part of Petrobrazi refinery’s broader modernization and transformation program.

“A modern electrical infrastructure is essential for the proper operation of a refinery. Through this investment, we are strengthening Petrobrazi’s electrical infrastructure to support both the refinery’s current operations and the new capacities under development, including SAF and HVO production as well as the green hydrogen projects. This is an important step in Petrobrazi’s transformation to meet the energy requirements of the future,” said Radu Caprau, member of the OMV Petrom Executive Board responsible for Refining and Marketing.

The project included the construction of a high-voltage power line directly connected to the Transelectrica substation, of a new-generation electrical substation, as well as a power distribution substation.

The new power infrastructure uses Blue GIS technology, a modern electrical switching system with a low environmental impact.

The refinery operates its own power generation unit, which currently supplies nearly all of its electricity needs.

A 7 MW photovoltaic energy project is also under construction at Petrobrazi.

The new electrical infrastructure creates the necessary conditions for integrating major projects currently under implementation, such as the production unit for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable diesel (HVO), as well as green hydrogen production capacities.

Petrobrazi refinery plays an important role in supplying the Romanian market with fuels and other petroleum products.

text:
Arcadia eFuels, a developer specializing in electric synthetic fuels, has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with energy company MB Energy to advance the decarbonization of European aviation. This strategic agreement seeks to establish a comprehensive infrastructure for the distribution, storage, and blending of synthetic aviation fuel (eSAF), addressing the urgent need for scalable, low-emission fuel solutions across Europe.

Building a Robust eSAF Value Chain

The partnership will focus on evaluating commercial and operational opportunities to create a resilient eSAF value chain throughout the continent. The initiative aims to integrate the entire process—from production using Power-to-Liquid technology to the final delivery of fuel to aircraft—thereby overcoming logistical challenges that have impeded the widespread adoption of sustainable aviation fuels. A central element of the collaboration is the development of a logistics framework encompassing transport, storage, blending, and delivery at major European airports. MB Energy will act as a strategic partner responsible for the purchase and distribution of eSAF volumes produced within the Arcadia eFuels project network.

Amy Hebert, CEO of Arcadia eFuels, emphasized the importance of a holistic approach, stating, “Commercializing eSAF requires more than simply producing sustainable fuel; it requires the entire value chain. MB Energy’s expertise in logistics, storage, blending, and fuel distribution makes it an ideal partner to connect production with the aviation market. Together, we are helping to build the infrastructure needed to expand the use of eSAF across Europe.”

Navigating Challenges in Sustainable Aviation Fuel Adoption

The push for synthetic aviation fuels coincides with increasingly stringent European regulatory frameworks prioritizing the decarbonization of air transport. However, the transition to eSAF faces significant hurdles. Meeting the rising demand for sustainable aviation fuel necessitates substantial investment not only in production capacity but also in the supporting infrastructure. The complexity of transporting, storing, and blending synthetic fuels—challenges mirrored in other regions such as the U.S. Midwest corn belt—highlights the critical need for resilient and efficient supply chains.

Moreover, the competitive landscape is evolving, with other companies likely to invest in similar infrastructure and production capabilities to secure market share. Geopolitical uncertainties, fluctuating tariffs, and escalating material and energy costs further complicate efforts to maintain supply chain resilience and sustainability.

Jonathan Perkins, CEO of MB Energy, underscored the importance of collaboration, noting, “The future success of synthetic fuels for aviation will depend on solid cooperation throughout the entire value chain. Arcadia eFuels brings its production expertise, while MB Energy contributes infrastructure, logistics, market access, and customer relationships. Together, our goal is to explore how to establish scalable and reliable eSAF supply chains for the European aviation market.”

This collaboration aligns with Arcadia eFuels’ broader strategy of forging alliances within the energy ecosystem to accelerate eSAF commercialization. For MB Energy, the partnership enhances its portfolio of low-emission solutions, reinforcing its role as a dependable energy provider amid a rapidly evolving market landscape.

text:
Bayer AG (Leverkusen, Germany) and Neste Oyj (Espoo, Finland), the world’s leading producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, have finalized a commercial agreement to jointly scale Bayer’s newgold® winter canola.

The collaboration will enable Bayer to significantly expand acres of winter canola in the Southern Great Plains of the U.S., strengthening the oilseed supply potential of lower-carbon-intensity feedstocks to meet the growing global demand for biofuels such as renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, which is estimated to increase almost threefold, reaching approximately 40 billion gallons by 2040. The high-protein meal from the winter canola grain will be sold into the feed market, offering additional feed sources for dairy and beef cattle, poultry, and swine markets.

“In times of geopolitical tensions, the need for more energy security and resilience while decarbonizing the transportation sector leads to growing demand for renewable fuel. This agreement further underscores Bayer’s commitment to help scale biofuels production,” said Frank Terhorst, Head of Strategy and Sustainability for Bayer’s Crop Science division. “We see the Southern Great Plains as an untapped opportunity for winter canola. The launch of newgold® winter canola will provide farmers with a profitable rotational crop with wheat and improve land utilization, while offering the opportunity to participate in a growing biofuels market.”

Bayer and Neste are establishing a newgold® network with additional value chain partners to support the expansion of winter canola and ensure an additional market for farmers.

“Maximizing the contribution of novel types of raw materials to support growth in renewables requires open supply chain collaboration. By building robust value chains, we can turn agricultural innovations into scalable realities for growers and energy markets. Through the Bayer newgold® winter canola collaboration, we are establishing a value chain in one of Neste’s key markets and developing opportunities to increase farm yields and grower income. This renewable raw material can be scaled rapidly in the coming years, which can help meet increasing biofuels demand,” said Artturi Mikkola, Senior Vice President, Renewable Products Feedstock Sourcing and Trading at Neste.

Bayer aims to launch newgold® winter canola hybrids in the fall of 2027. These hybrids offer farmers several benefits, including winter-hardiness, TruFlex®, Bayer’s second-generation Roundup Ready trait technology, and pod shatter resistance technology. Together, these advancements can deliver strong potential for yield performance and higher oil content. TruFlex winter canola, sold under the newgold® seed brand, will be designed with the goal of acting as a new profit opportunity for the Southern Great Plains, giving growers the flexibility to decide how and where it fits best in their operation.

text:
The billions of dollars worth of facility is entering the final investment decision stage and is seeking a strategic partner, with construction targeted to begin in 2027.

State-owned oil and gas company PT PERTAMINA is targeting 2029 for the start of Cilacap Bio-Refinery project's operations in Central Java, a facility designed to produce lower-emission fuels, including Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

The project requires an estimated investment of US$1.1 billion (Rp19.32 trillion). The development is currently undergoing the Final Investment Decision (FID) process alongside research for a suitable project partner.

PERTAMINA Patra Niaga Kilang Cilacap Executive General Manager Hermawan Budiantoro said the company is assessing potential partners as it moves toward construction.

"In 2026, we are conducting the FID and partnership process to determine the right partner to work with in building the biorefinery," Hermawan said at the Cilacap Refinery complex on Thursday, September 10, 2026.

The project began its engineering design phase through Front End Engineering Design (FEED) in 2025. Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) work is targeted to start in 2027, with the facility expected to come on stream in 2029.

SAF production and renewable feedstock

The biorefinery is planned to produce around 860 kiloliters (KL) of SAF per day or 870 KL of Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO) per day. The facility will occupy approximately 17.5 hectares (HA) within the Cilacap refinery complex.

PERTAMINA expects the project to significantly increase its biofuel production capacity, from about 27 KL per day currently to around 860 KL per day after the biorefinery is developed.

The facility will use plant-based and waste feedstocks, including used cooking oil (UCO), crude palm oil (CPO), and palm oil mill effluent (POME). Total feedstock requirements are estimated at about 311,000 tonnes annually.

"The benefit is supporting the energy transition by utilizing UCO or waste feedstock, turning materials that may no longer be used into useful and high-value products," Hermawan said.

SAF produced by the Cilacap biorefinery is planned to serve the aviation sector, with distribution targeted toward Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Tangerang and I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport in Bali.

text:
Why Is Sustainable Aviation Fuel Now a Boardroom Issue?

Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) has moved beyond being a niche aviation conversation. It is rapidly becoming a business, investment and ESG credibility issue for airlines, airports, fuel suppliers, logistics providers and multinational companies with significant travel emissions.

The urgency is real.

Aviation remains one of the harder sectors to decarbonise because long-haul aircraft cannot yet depend on batteries or hydrogen at commercial scale.

SAF—produced from sustainable waste, residues, biomass or synthetic pathways—offers a practical near-term route to lower lifecycle emissions without replacing today’s aircraft fleet or airport infrastructure.

Yet the central question remains: can supply grow quickly enough, affordably enough and credibly enough?

Is Supply Growing Fast Enough to Meet Aviation’s Climate Commitments?

Progress is visible, but the gap remains enormous.

Global SAF production rose from around 1 million tonnes in 2024 to an estimated 1.9 million tonnes in 2025.

For 2026, output is projected at approximately 2.4 million tonnes—still only around 0.8% of global jet-fuel consumption.

Meanwhile, aviation’s net-zero pathway will require SAF volumes on an entirely different scale over the coming decades.

This is not simply a production challenge. It is a feedstock, financing, policy and infrastructure challenge. Sustainable feedstocks are limited, competing industries are seeking the same renewable inputs, and next-generation e-SAF requires abundant low-carbon electricity, green hydrogen and captured carbon.

The transition will not be delivered by airlines alone.

Can SAF Compete When the Green Premium Is Still So High?

Cost remains the industry’s toughest obstacle.

SAF has commonly cost multiple times more than conventional jet fuel, creating a significant “green premium” at a time when airlines already operate in a highly competitive, margin-sensitive environment.

IATA estimates that SAF’s price premium added billions of US dollars to industry fuel costs in 2025.

This is where commercial leadership matters. Long-term offtake agreements, blended-finance structures, production tax incentives, carbon-pricing signals and corporate travel partnerships can help transform SAF from a costly voluntary purchase into a bankable market.

Businesses should view SAF not only as an environmental expense, but as a strategic hedge against future carbon costs, regulatory pressure and customer expectations.

Are Regulations Turning SAF into a Market Reality?

Policy is now reshaping demand.

In the European Union, ReFuelEU Aviation introduced a 2% SAF requirement from 2025, increasing to 6% by 2030 and progressing toward 70% by 2050.

The regulation is designed to stimulate supply while creating a more level competitive environment for aviation fuel suppliers and operators.

At a global level, ICAO’s CORSIA framework provides criteria and verification requirements for eligible fuels. This matters because credible SAF claims depend on lifecycle emissions data, sustainability certification and strong controls against double counting.

A lower-carbon fuel claim is only as strong as the evidence behind it.

What Does Credible ESG Disclosure Look Like for SAF?

For corporate buyers, aviation emissions are typically part of Scope 3 business-travel emissions.

Under IFRS S2, companies are expected to disclose material climate-related risks, opportunities, targets and Scope 1, 2 and 3 greenhouse-gas emissions using robust measurement approaches.

The standard builds on the TCFD architecture and requires companies to consider industry-based guidance, including SASB Standards.

The practical message is simple: do not report a SAF purchase as a feel-good statistic.

Explain the volume purchased, lifecycle-emissions methodology, certificate or registry approach, claim ownership, financial impact and alignment with the organisation’s transition plan.

Transparency will distinguish genuine climate action from attractive marketing.

Where Are Businesses Showing What Collaboration Can Achieve?

The most promising developments are increasingly collaborative.

Airbus and Cathay announced a co-investment partnership of up to US$70 million to help scale SAF projects in Asia and globally.

In France, Technip Energies, Airbus, Safran and Tereos formed a joint venture in June 2026 to develop a large-scale SAF project in Dunkirk—linking industrial capability, feedstock expertise and potential offtake demand.

These examples show the direction of travel: the winners will not merely buy SAF when available. They will help build the ecosystem that makes it available.

SAF is difficult, expensive and imperfect—but it is also essential.

The opportunity is not to wait for the perfect fuel. It is to create the partnerships, governance and investment confidence that allow sustainable aviation to take off.

KLM Cityhopper is celebrating its 60th anniversary, having developed from a small domestic carrier into a central component of KLM’s European network and Amsterdam Schiphol’s hub operation.

The airline began in 1966 as Nederlandse Luchtvaart Maatschappij (NLM), operating two leased Fokker aircraft on domestic routes. The Cityhopper name appeared in 1976, before mergers with NetherLines in 1991 and the subsequent integration of KLM UK created the present-day KLM Cityhopper.

Today, the regional subsidiary operates 58 aircraft to more than 80 destinations, conducting over 350 daily flights and carrying approximately 11 million passengers annually. Its services bring European travellers to Schiphol for onward intercontinental connections while distributing passengers arriving from around the world across Europe. Recent additions include Biarritz, Exeter, Dubrovnik, Ljubljana, Cork, Jersey, Santiago de Compostela and Oviedo.

KLM Cityhopper also serves as an innovation testbed for the wider KLM Group. Projects include virtual-reality pilot training, the OptiClimb fuel-saving application and trials involving artificial intelligence, sustainable aviation fuel, weight reduction, food-waste prevention and electrified ground operations.

After decades of flying Dutch-built Fokker aircraft, the airline began transitioning to Embraer in 2008. Embraer aircraft now form the backbone of its 58-strong fleet, including the quieter and more fuel-efficient E195-E2. KLM Cityhopper intends to continue modernising its fleet, optimising its network and adding European destinations.

text:
Glacier FarmMedia — Bayer is planning to expand canola acres in Oklahoma and elsewhere in the Southern Plains of the United States.

On Sept. 9, Bayer announced a partnership with Neste — a Finnish company that processes renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel — to increase production of winter canola in the region.

“This agreement further underscores Bayer’s commitment to help scale biofuels production. We see the Southern Great Plains as an untapped opportunity for winter canola,” said Frank Terhorst, head of strategy and sustainability for Bayer Crop Science.

WHY IT MATTERS

Global companies are developing partnerships to increase production of oilseeds in non-traditional growing regions to satisfy an exploding demand for biofuels.

Neste isn’t a familiar name to most Canadians, but the Finnish company produces renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel in 16 countries and has annual revenues of $31 billion.

Bayer and Neste are hoping to rapidly increase winter canola production in the Southern Plains, to satisfy the booming biofuel market.

“Global demand for… renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, which is estimated to increase almost threefold reaching approximately 40 billion gallons by 2040,” says the Bayer-Neste press release.

A key part of the commercial agreement between Bayer and Neste is that Bayer will launch a new variety of winter canola for the Southern Plains in the fall of 2027.

It will be part of Bayer’s newgold brand, a lineup of camelina and winter canola varieties that will connect agriculture to the “low carbon fuel economy,” said a Bayer release in February.

Second time charmed for canola?

In the early 2010s, canola was a hot crop in Oklahoma and southern Kansas. Growers in the region needed a crop to rotate with winter wheat and some agronomists touted winter canola as the solution. By the 2013-14 crop year, acres had reached 400,000 in Oklahoma, Kansas and parts of Texas. Optimism was through the roof, as some expected acres to top one million.

That optimism was short-lived, as cold winters and drought hammered the oilseed. Farmers abandoned winter canola and returned to growing wheat.

With wheat, growers in the Southern Plains could always depend on some yield. With winter canola, some years were a disaster,” said Ron Sholar, executive director of the Great Plains Canola Association, in 2020.

“With canola … you may not get anything. And that drove some (farmers) from it. It’s easier to fall back on wheat and that’s what they’ve done.”

Canola acres plummeted in Oklahoma and Kansas, sinking to about 10,000 to 20,000 per year.

Acres have picked up in the last few years, hitting about 40,000 in 2024.

Bayer and Neste are hoping that Bayer’s newgold winter canola will solve some of the agronomic challenges, which will convince growers to give canola another try.

Newgold winter canola will feature improved winter hardiness, TruFlex Roundup Ready traits and pod shatter resistance.

“Together, these advancements can deliver strong potential for yield performance and higher oil content,” Bayer said Sept. 9.

The idea behind Bayer’s newgold lineup is to provide another cropping option for farmers, so they have an oilseed that can be grown on marginal land. within existing rotations or as a second crop in the same year.
